title: Potential difference and energy transfer

learning_outcomes.text: define the potential difference across a component as the energy transferred per unit charge
recall and use V = W / Q

external_knowledge: Energy is measured in joules, J.
Charge is measured in coulombs, C.

prior_knowledge_summary: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge.
Use Q = It and Q = Ne.
Use I = Anvq to connect carrier motion with current.
Completed course module 9702_t09_cm01 Charge, current and drift.
new_learning: Potential difference measures energy transferred for each coulomb passing through a component.
not_yet_taught: e.m.f., internal resistance and network analysis

blocks.heading: The same charge, a different energy transfer
content: Imagine the same 2.0 C of charge passing through two components. One transfers 6.0 J and the other transfers 20 J. The amount of charge is identical, so what quantity distinguishes the components?
We need a measure of energy transferred for each coulomb that passes.

figure.purpose: Create the need for an energy-per-charge measure.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show two component boxes with equal 2.0 C charge packets entering. Label energy transferred 6.0 J and 20 J, but leave the comparison quantity unnamed.
figure.alt_text: Equal charge passes through two components that transfer different energies.

blocks.heading: Potential difference compares energy per charge
content: Definition to learn: potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge.

Potential difference is measured across a component. A potential difference of 5.0 V means the component transfers 5.0 J for every 1 C passing through it. The charge carriers continue through; they are not consumed.

figure.purpose: Connect one volt directly to one joule per coulomb.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show a component with charge packets crossing and energy arrows leaving. Add a scale card 5.0 J for each 1 C equals 5.0 V.
figure.alt_text: A component transfers five joules of energy for each coulomb passing through it.

blocks.heading: Use V = W/Q
content: V is potential difference in volts, V. W is energy transferred or work done in joules, J. Q is charge transferred in coulombs, C.
The unit relationship is 1 V = 1 J C^-1. This is a meaning check as well as a unit conversion.

figure.purpose: Teach formula symbols and the volt as joule per coulomb.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Use a formula triangle-style layout only as a memory aid beside a unit chain J divided by C equals V. Keep the full equation visible.
figure.alt_text: The equation V equals W divided by Q is paired with joules per coulomb.

blocks.heading: Interpret before and after calculating
content: A sensor transfers 18 J when 3.0 C passes through it. V = W/Q = 18/3.0 = 6.0 V.
Interpret the result: 6.0 J is transferred per coulomb. That sentence checks the calculation and gives the number physical meaning.
Reverse the equation when energy is required: W = VQ. For 0.40 C through 6.0 V, W = 6.0 × 0.40 = 2.4 J.

figure.purpose: Teach forward and reverse use with an interpretation check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show a worked layout V = 18 J divided by 3.0 C equals 6.0 V, then a second line W = 6.0 V times 0.40 C equals 2.4 J. Add a meaning box 6.0 J per C.
figure.alt_text: A worked example calculates potential difference, interprets it, then calculates energy.

blocks.heading: Potential difference belongs across a component
content: Current describes charge flow through a section. Potential difference describes energy transferred per unit charge across a component. These are related ideas, but they answer different questions.
Two components can have the same charge pass through them and transfer different energies. The one transferring more energy per coulomb has the greater potential difference.

figure.purpose: Contrast current through with potential difference across without teaching network rules.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Draw one isolated component. Put a charge-flow arrow through it and a bracket labelled potential difference across it. Add a two-row comparison table: current, charge flow; potential difference, energy per charge.
figure.alt_text: A component diagram contrasts current through it with potential difference across it.

blocks.heading: Voltage is not energy by itself
content: It is common to call potential difference an amount of energy. That misses the words per unit charge.
A 12 V component transfers 12 J only when 1 C passes. If 0.25 C passes, the energy is W = VQ = 12 × 0.25 = 3.0 J. Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge, not the total energy.

figure.purpose: Repair confusion between total energy and energy per charge.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Compare 1 C and 0.25 C passing through the same 12 V component, with energy transfers 12 J and 3.0 J. Use sparse charge packets.
figure.alt_text: Different charges passing through the same 12 volt component transfer different total energies.

blocks.heading: A three-step energy-per-charge method
content: First identify W, Q or V and convert units. Second choose V = W/Q or W = VQ. Third interpret volts as joules per coulomb and check that a larger charge at fixed V transfers proportionally more energy.
Use Q = It first if current and time are supplied, then carry Q in coulombs into W = VQ.
Stop at energy per charge. Power, resistance, e.m.f., internal resistance and network methods come later.

figure.purpose: Summarise the calculation route and safe boundary.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Flow chart: current and time optional to Q = It; W and Q to V = W/Q; V and Q to W = VQ; finish with J per C interpretation. No battery or resistor network.
figure.alt_text: A flow chart connects optional charge transfer to potential difference and energy calculations.

evidence_basis.evidence_scope_note: The direct potential-difference definition leaf is used. Mixed uniform-field leaves are retained as provenance but field equations and plate methods are excluded.

concepts_taught: potential difference as energy transferred per unit charge
forward and reverse use of V = W/Q
misconceptions_addressed: Potential difference is total energy rather than energy per charge.
Charge carriers are consumed when energy is transferred.
Potential difference is measured through rather than across a component.
next_lesson_can_assume: Use V = W/Q and W = VQ.
Interpret one volt as one joule per coulomb.
Use Q = It before W = VQ when current and time are supplied.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: P = VI or any electrical-power calculation.
E.m.f., internal resistance or circuit-network analysis.
